statement: A mandatory registry of large training clusters (or chip-location tracking) operates in >= 2 of the top-3 jurisdictions (official gazettes; by 2028-12-31)
status_at_phase_end: 0 of 3 operating at end-2024 under a strict reading; at most a partial 1 of 3. Bloc A collected cluster information through a one-off mandatory survey (Jan 2024) and proposed (not finalised) a standing quarterly reporting duty for clusters above 1e20 OP/s (Sept) and know-your-customer/reporting duties for cloud providers serving foreign AI training customers (Jan). Chip-location tracking existed only as a think-tank proposal. No Bloc B cluster registry or chip-tracking rule was found in this run (searched lightly).

items.summary: Bloc A proposed rules requiring cloud (IaaS) providers to verify foreign customers' identity and report when a foreign person trains a large AI model with potential malicious-cyber capabilities. A customer-reporting duty, not a cluster registry; proposed only.
items.detail: Bloc A BIS NPRM, 89 FR 5698 (FR Doc. 2024-01580), comments due 2024-04-29; implements EO 13984 and EO 14110 s.4.2(c).

items.summary: Bloc A proposed a standing quarterly notification duty for anyone acquiring, developing or possessing large-scale computing clusters (>300 Gbit/s networking and >1e20 OP/s theoretical peak for AI training), building on a mandatory survey issued 2024-01-26. Closest thing to a cluster registry in 2024, but proposed, not operating.
items.detail: Bloc A BIS proposed rule 89 FR 73612 (FR Doc. 2024-20529), 2024-09-11; definitions verified this run.

items.summary: A Bloc A policy think tank proposed 'on-chip governance mechanisms' (secure hardware features that could enforce or verify export-control policies on AI chips), citing chip smuggling. Policy proposal only; signals the chip-tracking idea entering mainstream debate.
items.detail: CNAS, 'Secure, Governable Chips: Using On-Chip Mechanisms to Manage National Security Risks from AI & Advanced Computing', 2024-01-08.
